narrative:
The model predicted an 86.7% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence. Being in the bottom decile for both Year 1 and Year 3 grades pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. These low rankings, compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students, signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 28 was the third most important factor. This score is well below the average of 37 seen among accepted students and also contributed to the prediction of failure, though less strongly than your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.5, family income in the middle bracket, full-time study plans, gender, and race played smaller roles. The model did not consider gender or race when making its decision.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to achieve a significantly higher score. Stronger grades and test results in a future application would directly address the factors that led to this rejection. (218 words)
